newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection begins in breast implant lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection begins in breast implant lawsuit.

text.p: Jury selection began on Monday for the first trial phase of a class-action lawsuit in which up to 10,000 Louisiana women seek damages from companies that manufactured, tested or sold silicone breast implants.

Orleans Parish District Civil Judge Yada McGee ruled that in this phase, with a subclass of an estimated 1,700 plaintiffs, the jury will decide if Dow Chemical Corp., half-owner of bankrupt implant-maker Dow Corning Corp., bears any responsibility for testing silicone as a medical device.
They also will decide if the company failed to disclose or even suppressed information on risks and if that kept recipients from making an informed decision about silicone breast implants.

Dow Corning was dismissed from the lawsuit because of bankruptcy proceedings. All claims against it will be handled by U.S. Bankruptcy Court. The case against Bristol-Meyers Squibb Co., another manufacturer, will be tried later.

If the jury determines that Dow Chemical bears some reponsibility for testing and safety, the same jury will be asked to decide if silicone caused injuries, if the recipients were aware of the risks and if they would have received the implants had they known all the dangers.

The third step, if the jury decides silicone caused medical problems, would be to notify potential class members. Another trial would be held grouping class members with similar illnesses. Class members would have to prove they would not have had the implants except for misrepresentations.

Lead plaintiffs' lawyer Dawn Barrios told Reuters the key issue was Dow Chemical's responsibility for testing silicone and component parts for Dow Corning, which had no toxicology lab and relied on Dow Chemical for safety information.
She said scientists found as early as the 1950s and 1960s that silicone migrates to the brain, liver and spleen and could be highly toxic.

"We're hoping for not only for sick women in Louisiana to be vindicated but to send a message to large chemical and medical companies that you can't put things in hunman bodies without adequate testing," Barrios said

Dow officials maintain the suit was filed only because the company has "deep pockets" for plaintiffs trying to obtain financial compensation. Company spokesman John Musser told Reuters Dow Chemical was nothing more than a shareholder in Dow Corning and its silicone testing was unrelated to breast implants. The company also maintains there is no scientific proof that silicones cause immune system problems.

An estimated 1 million American woman have received breast implants, roughly 80 percent of them for cosmetic reason. Many thousands claim they have suffered serious immune system diseases after the implants leaked or ruptured.
About 300,000 women received Dow Corning implants between 1962 and 1992, when the company ceased manufacturing them.
